The allegations against the petitioners were to the effect that with a view to cheating one Shamsuddin, the Petitioners in collusion with each other forged a document and used the same in Mutation Case No. 1606/9-1/77-78 dated 25-5-78 before the Revenue Officer. Following a charge-sheet submitted thereupon, a criminal case being DGR Case No. 19 of 1980 was ultimately started against the petitioners in the Court of the Additional District Magistrate, Rajshahi u/s 468/471 of the Penal Code. But on 24-6-84, the date fixed for appearance of the accused opposite-parties and framing of charge, the learned Additional District Magistrate discharged both the petitioners being of the view that the Revenue Officer holding mutation proceeding must be treated as a Court within the meaning of section 195 (1) (c) of the Code of Criminal Procedure and there being no complaint from him the taking of cognizance in the case was illegal. The learned Sessions Judge, Rajshahi was then moved in the matter by the State in Criminal Motion No. 222 of 1984. He took the view that a Revenue Officer could not be treated as a Presiding Officer of a Court and as such no complaint u/s 195 (1)(c) of the Code of Criminal Procedure was necessary in the case. Accordingly, by an order dated 21-1-85, the learned Sessions Judge set-aside the order of discharge and directed the learned Additional District Magistrate to proceed with the case according to law. This Rule has now been obtained by the accused-petitioners against the said order of the learned Sessions Judge. 

 "As pointed out in Halsbury's Laws of England, the word "Court" originally meant the King's Palace but subsequently acquired the meaning of (1) a Palace where justice was administered, and (2) the person or persons who administer it. In the Evidence Act, it is defined as including all Judges and Magistrates and all persons except arbitrators legally authorised to take evidence. This definition is by no means exhaustive and has been framed only for the purpose of the Act. There can be no doubt that to be a Court, the person or persons who constitute it must be entrusted with judicial functions, that is, of deciding litigated questions according to law. However, by agreement, between parties arbitrators may be called upon to exercise judicial powers and to decide a dispute according to law but that would not make the arbitrators a Court. It appears to me that before a person or persons can be said to constitute a Court, it must be held that they derive their powers from the state and are exercising the judicial powers of the State." 

 (2) such person or persons must derive the power of so deciding questions, from the State, and therefore will be exercising the judicial powers of the State ; and 

 11. This Court had also the occasion to analyse the different attributes of a Court in several decisions. In the case of IDBP vs M/s. Master Industries (1974) 26 DLR 157 and in the case of Shamsul Huq Sikder vs Election Tribunal & others, (1975) 27 DLR 388 it was laid down that "the exercise of judicial power of the State is the determining factor for investing a body with the character of a Court and that a Tribunal exercising a judicial power does not mean merely that it is acting with fairness and impartiality on a proper consideration of all relevant materials after giving an opportunity to all contending parties to present their respective cases. In order that exercise of judicial power or acting judicially may be a sign of acting as a Court, it must be acting as a part of the judicial machinery of the State, charged with the duty of determining the rights of one subject against another or a question of right between the subject and State and discharging its function according to established form of judicial procedure." 

 13. Mutation proceedings are done under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and the Rules framed thereunder. So let us now examine the provisions of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and the Rules framed thereunder, insofar as those relate to the powers and duties of a Revenue Officer and the procedure he follows in mutating one's name in the record-of rights. 

 14. Section 143 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act provides, inter alia, that the record-of-right prepared or revised shall be maintained up to date in the prescribed manner under Part IV, or under chapter XVII by correcting clerical mistakes and by incorporating the changes on account of (a) the mutation of names as a result of transfer or inheritance. 

 15. Chapter VI of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 consists of rules 22-25 of which rules 22-24 relate to mutation proceedings. Relevant portions of the said rules are reproduced be, low: 

 (2) In the cases of succession, intestate or testamentary the report shall contain the names and addresses of all heirs and their respective shares and nature of interests according to the law of inheritance applicable to the deceased or according to the terms of the testament, as the case may be, and also the description of the holding or holdings they have inherited. The report shall also state, if any, area of land inherited by any heir if acquirable under section 91 of the Act. 

 (3) In the case of alluvion, diluvion and reformation of land the report shall state its nature, area and location and, in the case of reformation or accretion, also the Khatian number of the holding to which it relates and the area which the raiyat concerned is entitled to possess under the provisions of section 86 or section 87 of the Act, as the case may be. 

 17. The view we have taken finds, support from the decision of the Privy Council in the case of Nirman Singh vs Thakurlal Rudra Protap Narain-Singh, AIR "1926 PC 100. In that case their Lordships held that mutation proceedings, is "in the nature of fiscal-inquiry instituted in the interest of the State for the purpose of ascertaining which of the several claimants for the occupation of certain denominations of immoveable property may be put into occupation of it with greater confidence that the revenue for it will be paid" and that it was an error to suppose that such proceedings are "judicial proceedings in which the title to and the proprietary rights in immoveable property are determined." 

 19. We are in full agreement, with the view expressed in the aforesaid decision. We are, therefore, of the opinion that a Revenue Officer dealing with a mutation proceeding under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and the Rule framed there-under does not constitute a Court. Since we have found that a Revenue Officer acting under Rule 23 of the Tenancy Rule is not a Court, it is needless for us to dilate on the question whether he is a civil, criminal or Revenue Court. 

 For the reason stated above we are of the view that the allegations in this criminal case do not attract the provisions of sections 195 (1)(c) Criminal Procedure Code. Accordingly we find no error in the order of the learned Sessions Judge.
